What's the last thing your team rebuilt three times before agreeing on it?

Your team can build faster than ever right now. So can everyone else's. 
That's the uncomfortable part of the AI shift nobody talks about enough. Speed stopped being the advantage, but deciding what to build, and staying aligned once you start, is where teams are actually losing ground.

On September 17, Douglas Ferguson (CEO, Voltage Control) joins us to unpack his "New Friction" thesis: AI made building cheap and moved the real bottleneck upstream, to deciding, aligning, and giving both people and AI agents the shared context to move together.

You'll leave with a working model for the three jobs that decide whether AI makes your team faster, or just busier.

posts.content:
Collaboration isn't always comfortable, and that's the point. Friction is what makes it work.

Dominik Katz, our Ways of Working Lead, believes collective intelligence has always run on friction — competing ideas grinding against each other until the strongest survives. Joan Miró — who gave this company its name — learned from Picasso and traded ideas with the Surrealists. Leonardo had Michelangelo. Shakespeare had Marlowe. The genius was never alone; the network made them.

AI is a new node in that network — and used well, it makes the whole thing smarter. Left unchecked, though, it smooths the friction away. It lets you skip the hard feedback, amplifies team misalignment, and takes no accountability for the outcome.

So how do we put the friction back?
Read Dominik's full piece: https://lnkd.in/eumNjKE9

document.title: Talktrack: Your better way to communicate

posts.content:
Love Tomorrow isn't a typical enterprise conference. It's built on the grounds of Tomorrowland, where thousands of people gather around ideas, creativity, and optimism. Not exactly where you'd expect to find a software company talking about the future of teamwork.

Which is exactly why we wanted to be there.

Rather than leading with product, we invited people to imagine the Team of Tomorrow. In our workshop, leaders from across industries picked up pens, paper, and scissors to sketch what collaboration between people and AI could look like. Those individual ideas were then brought together in Miro and synthesized into one shared artwork with Flows. It was a simple reminder that AI is at its best when it helps teams build on each other's thinking, not replace it.

Ben Crowe challenged us to think differently about leadership and mindset, while Dominik Katz reminded us that collective intelligence needs friction. Better ideas rarely come from instant agreement. They come from curiosity, different perspectives, and conversations that make us think a little harder.
That’s the future of work we believe in: not just faster individuals, but teams that think better together.

Thanks to everyone who joined us at Love Tomorrow! We can't wait to do it again.
